verses.translation_literal: And YHWH said to Noah: Go in, you and all your house, into the ark, for you I have seen righteous before me in this generation.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then the LORD spoke to Noah, and the word was an open door. "Come. Go into the ark, you and all your house. In all this generation, it is you I have seen standing righteous before me."
verses.directors_commentary: This is the first time God speaks to Noah since the building began, and the tone is invitation rather than command: 'Go in', not 'Build'. The work is finished, so the voice offers entry. The reason is stated as a verdict, not a reward: 'I have seen you righteous before me'. Play the pause after 'for you', because the Hebrew fronts the object, "you I have seen", and that stress is the whole point: out of a generation, one man. The KJV's 'for thee have I seen righteous' keeps the fronting but archaizes it; BBE's 'you only' adds a word that is not in the Hebrew, though it catches the stress. Note too that Noah is said to be righteous 'in this generation', a phrase the rabbis argued over: is he righteous only by comparison with his wicked age, or despite it? Rashi, drawing on Genesis Rabbah, notes that God praises Noah only in part when speaking to his face. 'Your whole house' reaches past Noah to his wife, sons and their wives, as 6:18 had promised.

philological_notes.note: Imperative of 'to come/go in'. After a long silence the first word God says to Noah in this scene is a verb of entering, not of doing: the work is over, and the ark is now a place to be, not to be built.
'Righteous'. In 6:9 Noah is 'righteous, blameless in his generations'; here only 'righteous' is repeated. Rashi reads this as the point that one praises only part of a man to his face.

verses.translation_literal: From all the clean animal you shall take for yourself seven seven, a man and his woman, and from the animal that is not clean it, two, a man and his woman.
verses.translation_dramatic: "Of every clean beast, take for yourself seven and seven, the male and his mate. And of the beasts that are not clean, take two, the male and his mate."
verses.directors_commentary: God now adds a detail the earlier command (6:19–20) left out: the animals are not all equal. Clean animals come in sevens; unclean ones in twos. The reason is practical and ritual at once: Noah will need animals to sacrifice (8:20) and to eat, and he cannot burn the last pair of a species. 'Clean' here anticipates the later Israelite food and sacrifice laws, long before Sinai, which is why Rashi said Noah had learned Torah. Notice the Hebrew says 'not clean' (lo' tehorah), not 'unclean', a small politeness that the rabbis read as a lesson in speaking cleanly (Radak records this). The KJV's 'by sevens' is fair, though the Hebrew repeats 'seven seven' in the distributive idiom, and the translators' 'the male and his female' softens the Hebrew, which says literally 'a man and his woman', the words used for human couples. Whether 'seven seven' means seven pairs or seven individuals is ancient debate; the flat Hebrew, with the contrast 'two', fits seven individuals, three pairs plus one for the offering.

philological_notes.note: Repeating a number makes it distributive: 'seven by seven', i.e. seven of each kind.
Literally 'a man and his woman', the vocabulary of human marriage, used for animal pairs. Radak explains that the Bible says ish ve'ishto where partners are fit to mate.
'Not clean', a deliberate avoidance of the word 'unclean'; Radak reports that the rabbis drew from this that a person should keep foul speech from his mouth.

verses.translation_literal: Also from the birds of the heavens seven seven, male and female, to keep alive seed upon the face of all the earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: "And of the birds of the sky, too: seven and seven, male and female, so that their seed may live on across the face of the whole earth."
verses.directors_commentary: Birds follow the same rule, and now the purpose is stated outright: 'to keep seed alive'. The ark is not a zoo but a seed bank. 'Seed' (zera') is the same word used for human descendants, so the verse ties animals and humans to one future. Rashi observes that the verse speaks only of clean birds, the unclean being understood from the previous verse. The KJV's 'fowls of the air' is archaic; 'birds of the heavens' is the Hebrew, and 'heavens' matters because in 7:11 the same heavens open. 'Upon the face of all the earth' is vast: the animals are being preserved so that the whole planet can be repopulated, not Noah's valley.

philological_notes.note: 'To make seed live / keep seed alive': a purpose clause, the stated aim of the whole rescue.

verses.translation_literal: For in seven days yet I am about to rain upon the earth forty days and forty nights, and I will wipe out every living thing that I have made from upon the face of the ground.
verses.translation_dramatic: "For seven days more, and then I send rain upon the earth: forty days and forty nights of it. And I will wipe away from the face of the ground every living thing I have made."
verses.directors_commentary: Now the clock starts. A week, then the rain. The Hebrew has the participle mamtir, 'I am about to rain', a word that makes the deed imminent and certain. The one verb 'rain' is chosen deliberately: the sky, not only the sea, is the weapon, and the threat is the undoing of Genesis 1, where God made everything. 'Wipe out' (machah) is the verb for wiping a dish clean or erasing writing, and the sound play is real: 'I made' (asiti) is taken back by 'I wipe' (machiti), the maker becoming the eraser. The KJV's 'every living substance' is a puzzling rendering of yekum, a word found only here and in Deut 11:6 in a related sense; it means whatever stands, whatever exists. Forty days and forty nights is the Bible's round number for a full testing period. Rashi, drawing on the Talmud, says the seven days were the mourning for Methuselah, whose death is calculated to fall at this very time; that is a rabbinic reading, not the plain text.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil participle of 'to rain': 'am causing it to rain'. The participle marks near, certain action.

'What stands, what exists', a collective for every living thing on the dry ground. Ibn Ezra notes the word occurs only in this passage; Radak takes the root as 'to arise', with an extra yod, and says it means land creatures only, not fish or those in the ark.
'And I will wipe out'; the verb of erasing. It answers 'which I have made' in the same verse.

verses.translation_literal: And Noah did according to all that YHWH had commanded him.
verses.translation_dramatic: And Noah did it. All of it, just as the LORD had told him.
verses.directors_commentary: Six Hebrew words, and no speech from Noah at all. Noah says nothing in this whole story; his obedience is his voice. The line echoes 6:22, which closes the building of the ark with almost the same words, and marks a second act of trust: first he built, now he enters. Play it flat and quick, since this is the quiet beat before the crowd of animals. The KJV 'according unto all' is accurate; BBE's 'did everything' loses the thorough 'according to' (ke-khol). Rashi reads the verse as Noah's entry into the ark, but the plain sense is wider: obedience in the preparation.

verses.translation_literal: And Noah [was] a son of six hundred years, and the flood was waters upon the earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: Noah was six hundred years old when the flood came: water over the earth.
verses.directors_commentary: A numeric pause in the narration. The Hebrew says 'son of six hundred years', the standard way of giving an age, and the flood arrives on its heels. The Hebrew for flood, mabbul, is a rare word used almost only for this event (and once of God's throne in Psalm 29:10); the KJV's 'flood of waters' is therefore right to keep the sense. The 'and' before the flood is a circumstantial 'when', as Radak explains. Ancient readers would have felt the age as enormous but also as exact: this is the old patriarch's last great act.

philological_notes.note: A rare word almost exclusive to the Flood story. Its root is uncertain (perhaps connected to Akkadian abubu, 'flood'). Radak notes it stands for 'flood of water'.

verses.translation_literal: And Noah went in, and his sons and his wife and the wives of his sons with him, into the ark, from the face of the waters of the flood.
verses.translation_dramatic: And Noah went in, and his sons with him, and his wife, and the wives of his sons, up into the ark, away from the face of the rising waters.
verses.directors_commentary: The family enters in the order of the household: Noah, sons, wife, daughters-in-law. The phrase 'from the face of the waters' is the vivid one, mipne, literally 'from before the face of', as if the flood were an advancing person who must be fled. The KJV's 'because of' flattens that image to a mere cause. Rashi picks up the sound of fear here: he reports a midrash that even Noah was 'of little faith' and entered only when the waters pushed him. Radak rejects this, since the text praises Noah. Rashi also notes the men and women are listed apart, which the midrash takes as a sign that marital relations were set aside while the world was in grief. These are rabbinic readings; the plain sense is simply a family, together, going in.

philological_notes.note: 'From the face of', i.e. 'because of / to escape'. It treats the waters as an approaching presence.

verses.translation_literal: From the clean animal and from the animal that is not clean, and from the bird, and all that creeps upon the ground,
verses.translation_dramatic: Of the clean beasts and the beasts that are not clean, of the birds, and of everything that crawls along the ground,
verses.directors_commentary: A list, read as a sweep of the camera over a crowd: clean, not clean, bird, creeper. The sentence has no main verb, so it hangs open until verse 9 finishes it with 'they came'. Play it as a long breath that gathers the world together. 'Creeps' (romes) is the verb used in Genesis 1 for the smallest land creatures, so the whole creation order is represented here again. The KJV 'fowls' and 'creepeth' are old but faithful. Note that the list again says 'not clean' rather than 'unclean'.

philological_notes.note: 'Creeping, crawling': small animals that move low across the ground, a category from the creation story.

verses.translation_literal: Two two, they came to Noah, to the ark, male and female, just as God had commanded Noah.
verses.translation_dramatic: Two by two they came, pair after pair, walking up to Noah and on into the ark, a male and a female of each, exactly as God had commanded Noah.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse opens on the numeral, doubled: shenayim shenayim, "two two". The Hebrew puts the pairs first and the arrival second, so the ear hears the animals as a procession before it hears that they came. The KJV, "There went in two and two unto Noah into the ark", keeps the active verb but fronts "There went in" and so loses that order; play the line with the pairs leading.

The verb "came" (bo'u) has the animals as the subject. Rashi reads this as "of their own accord", and Radak says they came to Noah by themselves and he brought them in, as commanded. Either way the actors who are animals should move as if summoned, not driven. "Male and female" is the ordinary pair of terms for sex in the Hebrew; the KJV's "the male and the female" adds an article the Hebrew does not have, which makes the pair sound like two particular animals. The closing "as God had commanded" uses Elohim, the general word for God; the chapter alternates it with YHWH (7:1, 7:5), and the shift to YHWH comes at 7:16.

philological_notes.note: Doubling expresses distribution: "two by two", pair after pair. English 'two and two' (KJV) is a fair rendering but loses the bare repetition that makes the sentence a procession.
"They came": the animals are the grammatical subject. The commentators disagree on whether this means they came on their own or were gathered by Noah.

verses.translation_literal: And it was at the seven of the days, and the waters of the flood were upon the earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: And when the seven days were done, the waters of the flood were upon the earth.
verses.directors_commentary: The week God promised has passed, and the narrator marks it quickly: the seven days of verse 4 are over. 'The waters of the flood' are now the grammatical subject; the verb 'were' is almost bare. After a week of loading animals, the silence before the storm breaks. The KJV 'after seven days' is a fair paraphrase. A week was also the normal period of mourning or of ritual waiting, which is why later readers tied it to Methuselah's death; Targum Pseudo-Jonathan states this openly, saying the waters came down boiling from heaven once his mourning was complete.

verses.translation_literal: In the six hundredth year of the life of Noah, in the second month, on the seventeenth day of the month, on this day all the springs of the great deep were split open, and the floodgates of the heavens were opened.
verses.translation_dramatic: In the six hundredth year of Noah's life, in the second month, on the seventeenth day, on that very day the world broke open. Every spring of the great deep burst its seal, and the sluices of heaven swung wide.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the hinge of the whole story, dated like a legal record: year, month, day. Ancient hearers knew that a date this exact belongs to a chronicle, a memory of fact. The disaster is two-fold and symmetrical: water rises from below, water falls from above. The cosmos of Genesis 1 had held back the waters above and below; now both barriers give way, and creation is run backwards. 'Split open' (nivqe'u) is a violent verb, used of cracking rock; the KJV's 'broken up' is weaker. 'The great deep' is tehom, the same word as the dark deep in Genesis 1:2, and the great deep here is feminine ('rabbah'), a point Radak and Ibn Ezra both note. The KJV's 'windows of heaven' translates 'arubbot', which are lattices or sluices, openings in a roof or dovecote, so 'floodgates' is closer; the Hebrew picture is of a lattice in the sky letting water through. The month is 'the second' without a name, and the rabbis argued whether it is Marheshvan (autumn) or Iyyar (spring). Rashi quotes both. Rashi also hears justice in 'great deep': they sinned in great (rabbah) wickedness and were punished by a great deep.

philological_notes.note: 'Were split, burst open': the verb used for splitting wood or rock, here for the earth's seals. Rashi: to let out their waters.

'The great deep'. Tehom is grammatically feminine here, as Radak and Ibn Ezra both observe; it echoes the deep of Genesis 1:2. Rashi hears a measure-for-measure play on 'great' wickedness (rabbah ra'at ha'adam, 6:5).
Lattices, sluices or openings; Ibn Ezra and Radak connect it to 2 Kings 7:2, where the same word is used of the heavens opening.

verses.translation_literal: And the rain was upon the earth forty days and forty nights.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the rain fell upon the earth, day and night, forty days and forty nights, without ceasing.
verses.directors_commentary: After the cosmic break of verse 11 the narration drops to a plain, almost weary beat: the rain was. The word here is geshem, ordinary rain, not mabbul, the flood; Rashi asks why, and answers that God sent it first as rain that could still have become blessing had people repented, and only when they did not did it turn into a flood. The 'forty days and forty nights' is the number promised in verse 4, and the doubling of 'forty' makes the time heavy: day, night, day, night. Rashi counts the first day out of the forty because the springs broke open on the same day. The KJV is accurate here; BBE's 'came down' adds a verb the Hebrew lacks. Keep the voice steady and unbroken, and let the repetition do the work.

philological_notes.note: Ordinary rain, as opposed to the mabbul. Rashi explains the choice of word: rain of mercy, which turned to flood only when the people did not return.

verses.translation_literal: On the bone of this day Noah went in, and Shem and Ham and Japheth, the sons of Noah, and the wife of Noah and the three wives of his sons with them, into the ark;
verses.translation_dramatic: On that very day, in the full light of it, Noah went in. His sons went in behind him, Shem and Ham and Japheth, and his wife, and the three wives of his sons beside them. One household, eight souls, and the great dark mouth of the ark swallowing them whole.
verses.directors_commentary:
The phrase is בְּעֶצֶם הַיּוֹם הַזֶּה, literally 'in the bone of this day'. The same idiom marks Abraham's circumcision (Gen 17:23) and the Exodus (Ex 12:41): it means 'on that very day', and it marks a fixed, public hour. Rashi reads it as a challenge: the generation of the flood said that if they saw Noah enter they would smash the ark and kill him, and God answered that He would bring him in before everyone's eyes, 'and we shall see whose word stands'. Play the entry as a public act, with onlookers.

The KJV's 'selfsame day' is sound but flattens the bodily image. Note the order: the men are named, then the wives, but the verse closes by gathering all into a single word, 'the ark' (תֵּבָה, the same rare word used for the basket of baby Moses). The ark is not a ship but a floating box, a chest, with no steering and no sail; the actors are not setting out on a voyage but being sealed in. Eight people: Noah, his wife, three sons, three daughters-in-law.

philological_notes.note: Idiom 'in the bone/very substance of this day', i.e. 'on that very day'. Marks a day as solemn and publicly witnessed.
'Ark, chest'. Used only for Noah's vessel and for the basket of the infant Moses (Ex 2:3); the word carries the sense of a sealed container that saves life, not a ship (which is אֳנִיָּה).

verses.translation_literal: They, and every living thing according to its kind, and every beast according to its kind, and every creeping thing that creeps on the earth according to its kind, and every flier according to its kind, every bird, every wing.
verses.translation_dramatic: And with them came the others, all of them, each after its own kind: the wild things of the field, the herds, the crawlers that drag their bellies over the ground, the fliers of the air. Every bird, every wing, down to the smallest beat of feathers, folded itself in under that roof.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse is a roll-call, built from the 'after its kind' formula of Genesis 1. The creation order of Day 5 and 6 is replayed here as an act of un-creation reversed: the same classes of life that God made are now being gathered back into a single box. Speak it as a litany, with the rhythm of repetition.

The last phrase, כֹּל צִפּוֹר כָּל כָּנָף, 'every bird, every wing', is deliberately redundant. Radak reads the three terms (עוֹף, צִפּוֹר, כָּנָף) as a widening scale, from large birds to the smallest winged things like locusts, wasps and flies. Rashi likewise takes כָּנָף to include locusts. The KJV's 'every bird of every sort' smooths the sound out and loses the repeated 'every'. It also renders חַיָּה as 'beast' and בְּהֵמָה as 'cattle', which is the right split: wild versus domesticated animals.

philological_notes.note: A figura etymologica: 'the creeper that creeps'. The noun and verb share a root, and the sound of the repetition mimics the crawl.
'Every wing': anything winged, which Radak extends to locusts, wasps and flies.

verses.translation_literal: And they came to Noah, to the ark, two two of all the flesh in which was the breath of life.
verses.translation_dramatic: They came to Noah, and through Noah to the ark, two by two, pair after pair, from every kind of flesh that carried the breath of life in it.
verses.directors_commentary:
'Two two' (שְׁנַיִם שְׁנַיִם) is the Hebrew way of saying 'in pairs', by simple repetition, with no preposition; the KJV's 'two and two' invents a conjunction. The animals come 'to Noah', not simply 'to the ark': Noah stands at the door as the one who receives them. Ramban stresses that the animals were not collected by Noah over a long time; they came on the day itself, summoned by God's command and spirit all at once. Radak, by contrast, says they came in the same pairs as on their first entry. Either way the scene is orderly, not a stampede.

The key phrase is רוּחַ חַיִּים, 'breath of life'. 'Flesh' (בָּשָׂר) here is a broad term: everything that lives and breathes. In the ancient Near East, breath was what distinguished living flesh from clay; this is Genesis 2:7 reversed into a rescue list.

philological_notes.note: Distributive repetition: 'two by two'. Hebrew has no 'and' between them.
'Breath of life', the animating wind; the criterion for who enters the ark.

verses.translation_literal: And those coming, male and female, from all flesh, they came, just as God had commanded him; and YHWH shut behind him.
verses.translation_dramatic: And so they came in, the male and the female of all flesh, every one as God had commanded him. And when the last had crossed the threshold, the LORD himself shut the door behind him.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse changes the name of God in mid-sentence. In the first half Elohim commands, the God of creation and of the order given to Noah; in the last three words YHWH closes the door. The chapter alternates the names (YHWH in 7:1 and 7:5, Elohim in 7:9 and 7:16a), so this is not the first appearance of YHWH, but here the shift is as sharp as it can be: the one who commanded is the one who acts. Let the voice change on "and YHWH shut".

The KJV's "the Lord shut him in" is close, but it turns "behind him" (ba'ado) into "in", a different picture. Rashi reads ba'ad as "against", the door shut to hold the water off; Radak, that God guarded him so that not one hole opened in the ark; Ibn Ezra, that this closing was a mercy, since an opened ark would have meant instant death. The Hebrew says only "behind him": for the ear, a door, a bolt, a silence. Nobody in the scene acts but God. After this, nothing Noah does can undo it.

The KJV "they that went in, went in male and female" is an accurate but clumsy echo of the Hebrew repetition ("those coming ... they came"). Zakhar and neqevah are the ordinary pair, the same words used of humans in Gen 1:27.

philological_notes.note: "And he closed/shut." The subject is YHWH; the verb is the same as for shutting a city gate or a door, which fits the ark's side door in 6:16.
"Behind him" or "on his behalf". Rashi takes ba'ad as 'against', as in other uses; Ibn Ezra and Radak hear protection.
"And female", from the root נקב, "to pierce, bore". It is the ordinary term for the female sex; the same pair, זָכָר וּנְקֵבָה, is used of humans in Gen 1:27.

verses.translation_literal: And the flood was forty days on the earth; and the waters multiplied and lifted the ark, and it rose from upon the earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: For forty days the flood lay upon the earth. The waters swelled, and swelled again, and then they took hold of the ark and lifted it. Slowly the great box rose, and the ground fell away beneath it.
verses.directors_commentary:
The word for flood is מַבּוּל, found in the Bible almost only in the Noah story (and once in Psalm 29:10, where it is God's throne). It is a technical, cosmic term, not an ordinary river-flood (which would be שֶׁטֶף). Radak notes that the 'forty days' means days and nights together, as in Genesis 1:5.

The verbs build a sequence of lifting: 'multiplied', 'lifted', 'rose'. The KJV's 'bare up' is archaic, and its 'above the earth' misses מֵעַל, 'from upon', i.e. the ark came off the ground. Rashi notes the ark sat about eleven cubits deep in the water, like a loaded ship, so it floated only when the waters were well over its draft. The point for the actors: before this moment the family was shut in but still earthbound; now the earth itself is gone.

philological_notes.note: The 'flood' or deluge, a rare word used almost only of Noah's flood; its derivation is debated.
'And it rose' (up, high): the ark is the grammatical subject, but the waters do the lifting.

verses.translation_literal: And the waters grew mighty and multiplied exceedingly on the earth, and the ark went on the face of the waters.
verses.translation_dramatic: The waters grew strong. They multiplied past all measure over the earth, and the ark went out across the face of the deep, alone, a single moving thing on a world of water.
verses.directors_commentary:
Two verbs of growth, גָּבַר and רָבָה, are piled up. גָּבַר is a word of strength (from the root of 'hero', גִּבּוֹר), so the waters do not merely rise but gain power. Radak says that 'grew mighty' is stronger than 'multiplied', and the verse uses both to show that the flood increased in force as well as in quantity. Ramban adds that the waters came with violence, uprooting trees and toppling buildings.

The ark 'went' (וַתֵּלֶךְ), the ordinary verb of walking; the KJV's 'went upon the face of the waters' is correct and I would keep it. The BBE's 'was resting' is wrong: the ark is moving, though without steering (Sforno says it was driven by the surge from below). The picture is of a vessel without rudder or sail, carried by the current alone.

philological_notes.note: 'They prevailed, grew mighty'; a word of strength, not just height, used again in 7:19, 7:20 and 7:24 as a refrain.

verses.translation_literal: And the waters grew mighty, very, very much, on the earth; and all the high mountains that were under all the heavens were covered.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the waters grew mighty, mighty beyond all measure, over the earth, until every high mountain beneath the whole sweep of heaven lay buried.
verses.directors_commentary:
'Very, very' (מְאֹד מְאֹד) is the Hebrew superlative by doubling; the KJV reads 'exceedingly' and loses the drumbeat. The verse is the climax of the rising, and the actors should let the voice climb with it.

The KJV has 'hills' for הָרִים, but the Hebrew word means 'mountains', and the phrase 'under all the heavens' is deliberately total: the text claims that no peak remained. Ibn Ezra writes that we believe the words of our God and dismiss the claims of men about some high mountain. The idiom 'under all the heavens' is the ancient way of saying 'everywhere'. A flood that covers the mountains is a return to the watery deep of Genesis 1:2.

philological_notes.note: Doubling for the superlative: 'very, very much'.
'Under all the heavens' = the whole inhabited world, a merism for totality.

verses.translation_literal: Fifteen cubits upward the waters grew mighty, and the mountains were covered.
verses.translation_dramatic: Fifteen cubits above them the waters rose in their strength, and the mountains lay covered, drowned beneath it.
verses.directors_commentary:
A measurement, in a story that has run on size and number: the flood is given a figure. Fifteen cubits is roughly 6.5 to 7 metres (taking a cubit as about 45 cm, an approximate modern equivalent; cubits varied), about the height of a two-storey house. The KJV's "Fifteen cubits upward did the waters prevail" is faithful, but the verb gavru, "grew mighty", is the same verb used in 7:18-19: the waters are not merely high, they are strong. Keep the repetition audible.

The measure can be heard two ways. Rashi takes it as the height above the mountaintops, once the water stood level with the peaks; Radak, that it says how far the water rose over the mountains, and then "the mountains were covered" is the result, even the high ones. The Hebrew does not decide between them; play it as the narrator giving a figure that is meant to feel final.

philological_notes.note: "Cubit", the forearm length from elbow to fingertip, about 45 cm (an approximate modern equivalent; its exact value varied).
"From above, upward". Whether the fifteen cubits count above the peaks or define how deep the cover was is left open in the verse; Rashi reads it as above the peaks.

verses.translation_literal: And all flesh that creeps on the earth expired: among the fliers, and among the beasts, and among the wild animals, and among all the swarmers that swarm on the earth, and every human.
verses.translation_dramatic: And everything that moved upon the earth breathed its last: birds, herds, wild things, every swarming creature that crawled over the ground. And last of all, humankind.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verb וַיִּגְוַע, 'expired', is a gentle verb of death, 'breathed out his last'; it is used of Abraham, Ishmael and Isaac (Gen 25:8, 17; 35:29). The KJV's 'died' is plain; Radak says it means a swift death without lingering, like a drowning. Ibn Ezra takes it as a completed event ('had expired').

The list moves from the sky to the ground and ends on the human: 'and every human', וְכֹל הָאָדָם, placed last. Radak comments that the human is named last on purpose: even he, with his intelligence and his ability to climb to the highest peaks, was not saved. The list reverses Genesis 1:20-27, in which the creatures were made in the same classes, ending with the human, so the creation order is undone line by line. The wording 'swarmer that swarms' (שֶׁרֶץ הַשֹּׁרֵץ) echoes the 'creeper that creeps' of verse 14.

philological_notes.note: 'And he/it expired': a solemn verb for dying, applied to the patriarchs; it denotes a quick death by breathing one's last.
'The swarmer that swarms': noun and verb from the same root, as with 'creeper that creeps'.

verses.translation_literal: All in whose nostrils was the breath of the spirit of life, of all that was on the dry ground, died.
verses.translation_dramatic: Everything that had drawn the breath of life through its nostrils, everything that stood on dry ground, was dead.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the most anatomically specific line of the chapter: 'in his nostrils'. The Hebrew phrase is נִשְׁמַת רוּחַ חַיִּים בְּאַפָּיו, a double construct ('breath of the wind of life') that has no clean English equivalent. Radak reads the two as 'breath of life and wind of life', that is, נשמה for the human and רוח for animals; the KJV and BBE simply drop one. The nostrils recall Genesis 2:7, where God breathed into the man's nose; the flood is that breath withdrawn.

Note the limit: 'on the dry ground' (בֶּחָרָבָה). Rashi and Radak both say this spares the fish, which live in water. The word חָרָבָה is the same as the dried land of Genesis 8:13, so the ground has already become, in language, what it will be afterwards. The KJV's 'dry land' is correct.

philological_notes.note: A double construct, 'breath of the spirit of life'. Radak separates human 'neshamah' from the animals' 'ruach'.
'On the dry ground': the limiting phrase that excludes sea creatures.

verses.translation_literal: And he wiped out all the living-thing that [was] on the face of the ground, from man unto beast, unto creeping-thing and unto bird of the heavens, and they were wiped out from the earth; and only Noah was left, and those who [were] with him in the ark.
verses.translation_dramatic: And so He wiped it away: every living thing that had moved upon the face of the ground. Man, beast, creeping thing, the bird of the heavens, none was spared the sweep of it. Wiped out, and wiped from the earth itself, until the world held no trace of them. Only Noah was left, and those who were with him in the ark, rocking on the water in a silence with nothing else in it.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse says the same thing twice on purpose. First God is the subject: 'he wiped out' (וַיִּמַח, Qal). Then the creatures are: 'they were wiped out' (וַיִּמָּחוּ, Niphal). The verb מָחָה is the one for wiping a dish clean or blotting out writing, so the picture is a slate wiped, a scribe's erasure, not a battle. It echoes God's decision in 6:7, 'I will wipe out man whom I created', and the sentence now closes that loop. Play the first verb as the act and the second as the result.

The tradition asked why the doubling. Ibn Ezra and Radak read וַיִּמָּחוּ as total erasure of memory: no seed, no building, no 'this house was built by so-and-so who died in the flood' (Radak). Ramban reports that reading as others' view and questions it, since nothing needs saying about seed after everything has died; he proposes instead that the second verb tells us that not even the eggs of birds and of some creeping things survived, in trees or under the ground. Rashi, for his part, only fixes the grammar: וַיִּמַח is an active form, 'he wiped out', not a passive. The rabbis in Sanhedrin 108, which Ramban and Radak cite, split the verbs between this world and the world to come.

The KJV's 'every living substance was destroyed' softens the picture twice. It turns an active, personal 'he wiped out' into a passive, and it uses 'destroyed' for both verbs, so the doubling disappears. 'Substance' is also archaic for יְקוּם, a rare word meaning something that stands up, a living being. Sforno takes it to mean animal life, not plants. Note also 'Noah only remained alive': the Hebrew has no 'alive'; it says 'was left' (וַיִּשָּׁאֶר), the word of a remnant. Ibn Ezra points to this verse as the flat refutation of anyone who calls the flood local.

The merism 'from man to beast to creeping thing to bird of the heavens' mirrors the creation list in Genesis 1, run backwards: the world has been un-made in the order it was made. The sentence ends on a small band of survivors, 'Noah and those with him', and the last word, the ark, is all that floats.

philological_notes.note: Qal wayyiqtol of מָחָה, 'wipe, blot out'. God is the agent. Rashi stresses that this is the active form (vayyifal) and not the passive, like וַיִּפֶן and וַיִּבֶן from final-he verbs; the hireq under the yod is the mark.

A rare noun. My own reading of the root קום ('to stand, rise') is that it names what stands up, a living being. Sforno narrows it to animate creatures, as the list that follows shows, and excludes plants.

Niphal of the same root, answering the Qal. Ibn Ezra and Radak: even their name and memory were wiped out, for they have no seed or building left. Ramban reports that reading as others' and doubts it, suggesting the doubling means not even the eggs of birds and creeping things remained. Rabbinic exegesis (Sanhedrin 108): wiped out of this world and of the world to come.

'Only Noah', a restrictive particle that sets the survivor against the whole list before it. Rashi gives 'Noah alone' as the plain sense and records a Midrash that he was ill from the labour of feeding the animals.

verses.translation_literal: And the waters grew mighty on the earth a hundred and fifty days.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the waters held their might over the earth, a hundred and fifty days.
verses.directors_commentary:
The chapter ends on a number, as it began with one (Noah's six hundred years). A hundred and fifty days is five months of thirty days, the length the later calendar of the flood story counts from the 17th of the second month to the 17th of the seventh (Gen 8:4). Radak and Sforno disagree whether the 150 days include the first forty of rain; the text says only that the waters 'prevailed' for that span. Ibn Ezra adds that the rain did not stop and start but that the springs of the deep kept the flood strong.

The verb is again גָּבַר, the refrain of the chapter (7:18, 19, 20, 24). Tone: after the intensity of the deaths, a flat, almost exhausted counting, with the ark shut in the dark and no one able to see the sky. Radak, asking how Noah could count days without sun or stars, suggests he kept time with lamps and an instrument.

philological_notes.note: 'They prevailed', here the refrain verb for the total period of the flood's strength.

events.title: The LORD tells Noah to enter the ark
events.narrative_summary: The LORD tells Noah to go into the ark with his household because he is righteous, to take seven pairs of clean animals and birds and two of the unclean, and announces rain in seven days for forty days and nights.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 7:4 gives 'yet seven days' before the rain. The rain starts on the 17th of the second month of Noah's 600th year (7:11): 1 month (29.53 d) + 16 d = 45.53 days from the start of anchor.flood. Minus seven days gives 38.53 days. Margin of about one day: the only slack is how the month is reckoned (29.53-day synodic average against 29 or 30 days) and the hour of the day. The Tishri/Nisan dispute (Rashi on 7:11) moves the season of the year, not this offset. Rashi and Radak read the seven days as Methuselah's mourning; the text states only the delay.

events.title: Noah does all that the LORD commanded
events.narrative_summary: Noah does everything the LORD commanded him.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Read as the seven-day period of preparation between the command (7:4) and the rain (7:10), after Radak, who has Noah stock and arrange the ark in this week. Starts when the command ends and lasts 167 hours so that the entry falls 7 days after the command. Margin 6 hours.

events.title: Noah, aged 600, and the animals go into the ark
events.narrative_summary: Noah, six hundred years old, enters the ark with his sons, his wife and his sons' wives, because of the flood waters, and the clean and unclean animals, birds and creeping things come to him two by two.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 7:6 gives Noah's age, the year of the Flood; 7:13 says this entry took place on the very day the waters came (the 17th of the second month, 7:11), seven days after the command (7:10). Placed at the end of the preparation week, 45.53 days from the start of anchor.flood. Duration of a few hours is an estimate for the boarding. Radak places the entry at the start of the week instead.
events.ancient_year_marker: When Noah was six hundred years old

events.title: The springs of the deep burst and the floodgates of heaven open
events.narrative_summary: After the seven days, on the seventeenth day of the second month of Noah's six hundredth year, all the springs of the great deep burst open and the windows of heaven are opened.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 7:10 'after seven days' and 7:11 'in the second month, the seventeenth day, on this day'. Starts the moment the door is shut (same day, 7 days and a few hours after the command, Radak on 7:13). Duration one hour is nominal. Rashi on 7:11: the month is Marcheshvan (R. Eliezer) or Iyar (R. Joshua).
events.ancient_year_marker: In the six hundredth year of Noah's life
events.ancient_season_marker: In the second month, on the seventeenth day

events.title: Rain falls on the earth forty days and forty nights
events.narrative_summary: The rain falls on the earth for forty days and forty nights.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 7:12 and 7:4 give forty days and nights, beginning on the day the floodgates opened (7:11). Starts with the opening; the text's duration is used. Rashi: the first day is not counted because its night belongs to the previous Hebrew day, a matter of a day only.

events.title: On that same day all enter and the LORD shuts the door
events.narrative_summary: On the very day, Noah, his sons, his wife and the sons' wives enter the ark, with every kind of animal, male and female as God had commanded; then the LORD shuts the door behind him.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 7:13 'on the very day' ties this to the day of 7:11. It is the same boarding as 7:7-9, told with the day and the closing of the door; it starts with that boarding and lasts four hours, ending with the door shut. Margin 3 hours.

events.title: The waters rise and lift the ark above the earth
events.narrative_summary: As the flood continues forty days on the earth, the waters grow and lift the ark high above the land.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 7:17 places the rise within the forty days of flood. The day is not given: start estimated 10 days after the rain began with margin 10 days, lasting the remaining 30 days of the forty.

events.title: The waters prevail on the earth for a hundred and fifty days
events.narrative_summary: The waters surge and swell far above the earth, the ark floats on their surface, and the waters prevail for a hundred and fifty days.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 7:24 states 150 days. Sforno counts them from the first day of the rain (17th of the second month) to the 17th of the seventh month, five full months of 30 days (cf. 8:4). Anchored on the start of the flood, duration from the text, margin one day.

events.title: The waters cover the highest mountains
events.narrative_summary: The waters swell until all the high mountains under the whole heaven are covered, fifteen cubits deep.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: No date is given in 7:19-20. The waters peak at about the end of the forty days of rain, so 40 days after the start, margin 20 days, one day long. The 15 cubits is a depth, not a time.

events.title: All flesh on dry land dies; only Noah and those in the ark remain
events.narrative_summary: Every creature that moved on the earth dies, birds, livestock, wild animals, swarming things and all humankind, everything with the breath of life on dry land. The LORD wipes out every living thing, leaving only Noah and those with him in the ark.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: No day is given. The deaths come as the waters rise over the land: estimated to start 10 days after the rain began, lasting 30 days, margin 10 days, inside the 150 days of prevailing.

causal_edges.causal_explanation: The LORD's announcement that he would bring the flood on the earth (6:17) comes true when the deep bursts and the heavens open (7:11).
The animals and the family come in as God had commanded in the ark instructions (6:18-20; 7:9, 7:16).
The finished ark made it possible for the LORD to tell Noah to enter it (6:22; 7:1).
The rain and the bursting springs make the waters increase until they lift the ark (7:17).
The LORD's word that he would wipe out every living thing he had made (7:4) is fulfilled when all flesh dies (7:21-23).
Noah goes into the ark because the LORD told him to come in with his household (7:1, 7:5, 7:9).
The LORD's word that in seven days he would send rain for forty days and nights (7:4) is fulfilled in 7:12.

entities.etymology_meaning: A collective label for the land animals, creeping things and birds that come to Noah, in pairs or by sevens, according to their kind.
entities.summary_bio: The beasts, creeping things and birds that go into the ark with Noah. Clean animals and birds come by sevens, the unclean by pairs, male and female, so that their seed is kept alive.

aliases: the deep and the windows of heaven
entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew mabbul is used almost only of this flood; its root is uncertain, perhaps related to a Mesopotamian word for flood.
entities.summary_bio: The waters that come from the springs of the great deep and the floodgates of heaven. They rise until they lift the ark and cover the highest mountains, and they hold the earth for a hundred and fifty days.

components.evidence_explanation: Gen 7:16 says the LORD shut him in.
Gen 7:17 says the waters lifted the ark and it rose above the earth.
Gen 7:10 says the waters of the flood were upon the earth.

components.label_value: All perished except those in the ark
components.evidence_explanation: Gen 7:21–23 says every human on dry land died and only Noah and those with him remained.
Gen 7:7 says Noah went into the ark because of the waters of the flood.

systems.name: Clean and unclean animals
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Israelite tradition divided animals into those fit for sacrifice and food and those that were not; Genesis shows the distinction already in Noah's time, before the Sinai laws, and the clean animals are later the ones offered (Gen 8:20).
rules_and_mechanics: Clean animals are taken in larger numbers than unclean ones.
The distinction is announced by God and carried out by Noah.
Pairs are male and female, so that offspring can continue.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Every creature with the breath of life on dry land dies, from humans to birds, and only Noah and those with him in the ark are left.
system_instances.significance_note: The announced judgment is carried out in full, leaving a single remnant.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Noah is told to take clean animals and birds by sevens and unclean animals by pairs, male and female.
system_instances.significance_note: It prepares for the offerings after the flood and for keeping every kind alive.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The LORD tells Noah to enter the ark with his household and says that in seven days he will send rain for forty days and nights.
system_instances.significance_note: The command rests on Noah's righteousness and starts the final stage of the flood story.

system_instances.outcome_summary: The springs of the great deep are split open and the floodgates of heaven are opened on the seventeenth day of the second month.
system_instances.significance_note: Waters come from above and below at once; the opening of the deep and the windows of heaven is often read as undoing the separation of the waters in Gen 1:6-9.

edges.description: Noah does everything the LORD has commanded him.
The rising waters lift the ark above the earth.
The LORD commands Noah to enter the ark with all his household because he has seen him righteous.
The LORD closes the door of the ark behind Noah.
God wipes out every living thing on the ground, from humans to birds.
